title: GPT series and scaling laws
text:
CHAPTER 18. TRANSFORMERS
SECTION 18.3. THE GPT SERIES AND SCALING LAWS

BERT (Section 18.2) showed the power of pretraining for understanding tasks. A parallel line of work at OpenAI took the other branch of the transformer, the decoder, and trained it only to predict the next token. Through GPT, GPT-2 and GPT-3, models grew from about a hundred million parameters to 175 billion, and two discoveries emerged: very large language models could perform new tasks just from instructions or examples written in their input, and their performance improved predictably, following simple power laws, as parameters, data and compute increased. These "scaling laws" turned AI progress into something like an engineering plan, and set off the race to build ever-larger models that led to ChatGPT (Chapter 19).

1. The language modeling objective

A decoder-only transformer models the probability of a token sequence x_1, ..., x_T by the chain rule:

    P(x_1, ..., x_T) = product_t P(x_t | x_1, ..., x_(t-1))

and is trained to minimize the average negative log-likelihood (cross-entropy) per token:

    L = -(1/T) sum_t log P(x_t | x_<t)

With causal masking (Section 18.1), all T predictions in a sequence are trained in parallel. The loss is often reported as perplexity, exp(L): a perplexity of 20 means the model is, on average, as uncertain as if choosing uniformly among 20 tokens. To generate text, sample a token from P(x_t | x_<t), append it, and repeat; the "temperature" T_s rescales the logits z before the softmax, softmax(z / T_s), with lower values giving more predictable text. Nucleus (top-p) sampling (Ari Holtzman and colleagues, 2019) samples only from the smallest set of tokens whose total probability exceeds p.

Why would next-token prediction lead to general abilities? To predict text well, a model must capture grammar, facts, the style of different genres, and some of the reasoning that produced the text. The text of the internet contains translations, question-answer pairs, arithmetic, code and arguments, so a good enough predictor must model all of them.

2. GPT (2018)

"Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training" (Alec Radford, Karthik Narasimhan, Tim Salimans and Ilya Sutskever, June 2018) trained a 12-layer transformer decoder (768-dimensional states, 12 attention heads, about 117 million parameters, a size usually quoted for it) on the BooksCorpus, about 7,000 unpublished books, chosen because its long passages of continuous text let the model learn long-range structure. Fine-tuned with a small task-specific head, it improved the state of the art on 9 of 12 tasks studied. The paper also noted early signs of "zero-shot" behavior: the pretrained model, without fine-tuning, could do some tasks through heuristics, and this improved steadily during pretraining.

3. GPT-2 (2019)

"Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners" (Radford, Jeffrey Wu, Rewon Child, David Luan, Dario Amodei and Sutskever), announced on 14 February 2019, scaled up both model and data. The dataset, WebText, was built from outbound links on Reddit that had received at least 3 karma, used as a rough signal that humans found the page interesting; after cleaning, it contained slightly over 8 million documents, about 40 GB of text, with Wikipedia removed to avoid overlap with test sets. The largest model had 1.5 billion parameters (1,542M), with smaller versions of 117M, 345M and 762M.

The paper's main claim was that a language model trained on diverse enough text begins to perform tasks without explicit supervision, if the task is expressed in text. For summarization, append "TL;DR:" to an article; for translation, prompt with example pairs "english sentence = french sentence"; for question answering, write the question followed by "A:". Zero-shot, GPT-2 achieved state-of-the-art results on 7 of 8 language modeling benchmarks it was tested on, and nontrivial but far from state-of-the-art results on tasks like reading comprehension, summarization and translation. Performance improved steadily (roughly log-linearly) with model size, and the largest model still underfit WebText, suggesting further gains from scale.

GPT-2 is also remembered for its release strategy. OpenAI initially released only the smallest model, citing concerns about misuse such as generating fake news or spam, and released larger versions in stages, with the full 1.5B model released on 5 November 2019. The decision was debated: some praised it as a responsible precedent, others considered the risk overstated or the announcement a publicity effort. It started the continuing discussion of how and when to release powerful models.

4. GPT-3 (2020) and in-context learning

"Language Models are Few-Shot Learners" (Tom Brown and some thirty co-authors, arXiv 28 May 2020) introduced GPT-3: 175 billion parameters, 96 layers, model dimension 12,288, 96 attention heads, and a context window of 2,048 tokens. It was trained on about 300 billion tokens drawn from a filtered version of Common Crawl, an expanded WebText, two book corpora and English Wikipedia, with higher-quality sources sampled more often than their size alone would imply. Training used a cluster of NVIDIA V100 GPUs provided by Microsoft.

Compute: a common estimate for training a dense transformer is C approx 6 N D floating-point operations, where N is the number of parameters and D the number of training tokens (about 2 N D for the forward pass and 4 N D for the backward pass). For GPT-3: 6 x 175 x 10^9 x 300 x 10^9 = about 3.15 x 10^23 operations. The paper itself describes the cost as several thousand petaflop/s-days (one petaflop/s-day is 10^15 operations per second for a day, about 8.64 x 10^19 operations), consistent with this estimate.

The paper's central idea was in-context learning. Instead of fine-tuning, the task is shown to the model in its prompt:

    zero-shot:  "Translate English to French: cheese =>"
    one-shot:   one solved example, then the question
    few-shot:   several (often 10 to 100) solved examples, then the question

No weights are updated; the model infers the task from the context. GPT-3's few-shot performance was competitive with fine-tuned state-of-the-art models on some benchmarks (for example some question answering datasets) and far behind on others (some reading comprehension and natural language inference tasks). Crucially, the gap between zero-shot and few-shot performance grew with model size: larger models were much better at using examples in context. GPT-3 could do multi-digit addition (well for two or three digits, much worse for more), unscramble words, use a novel word in a sentence after seeing its definition, and write news articles that human evaluators could distinguish from real articles only at close to chance level in the paper's experiment.

The paper also documented limits: repetition and loss of coherence over long passages, poor performance on some commonsense physics questions, test-set contamination concerns (web data may contain benchmark questions), and biases relating to gender, race and religion.

OpenAI offered GPT-3 through a paid API starting in June 2020, rather than releasing the weights, and licensed it exclusively to Microsoft. Developers built writing assistants, chat bots and coding tools on the API, and a GPT descendant fine-tuned on code, Codex (2021), powered GitHub Copilot.

5. Scaling laws

In January 2020, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish and colleagues at OpenAI published "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models." Training many transformer language models of different sizes, they found that test loss follows power laws in each resource, when the others are not limiting:

    L(N) = (N_c / N)^alpha_N,     alpha_N approx 0.076,  N_c approx 8.8 x 10^13 non-embedding parameters
    L(D) = (D_c / D)^alpha_D,     alpha_D approx 0.095,  D_c approx 5.4 x 10^13 tokens
    L(C_min) = (C_c / C_min)^alpha_C,  alpha_C approx 0.050

(loss in nats per token). These trends held over more than six orders of magnitude, while architectural details such as depth versus width mattered relatively little. A small exponent means slow but steady improvement: with alpha_N = 0.076, multiplying the parameter count by 10 multiplies the loss by 10^(-0.076), about 0.84, a 16 percent reduction. Using the fitted constants, a 1-billion-parameter model has predicted loss (8.8 x 10^13 / 10^9)^0.076, about 2.38 nats, and a 10-billion-parameter model about 1.99. Power laws plot as straight lines on log-log axes, which is why charts in these papers look like ruler-drawn lines.

Two practical conclusions drove the industry. First, results could be predicted: by training small models, one can forecast the loss of a much larger one before spending the money. (The GPT-4 technical report, 2023, said OpenAI predicted aspects of GPT-4's final loss from models trained with much less compute.) Second, Kaplan and colleagues concluded that, for a fixed compute budget, most of the increase should go to model size, with data growing more slowly, which encouraged very large models trained on relatively few tokens per parameter.

6. Chinchilla: compute-optimal training

In March 2022, Jordan Hoffmann and colleagues at DeepMind ("Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models") revisited this question with over 400 models, also varying learning rate schedules to match the training length. They found that model size and training tokens should be scaled in equal proportions: for every doubling of model size, the number of training tokens should also double. In practice this works out to roughly 20 tokens per parameter. By that measure, models like GPT-3 (175B parameters, 300B tokens, under 2 tokens per parameter) and DeepMind's own Gopher (280B) were heavily undertrained.

To test this, they trained Chinchilla, with 70 billion parameters and 1.4 trillion tokens, using the same compute budget as Gopher (6 x 70 x 10^9 x 1.4 x 10^12 = about 5.9 x 10^23 operations). Chinchilla uniformly and significantly outperformed Gopher, GPT-3 and other larger models on a wide range of evaluations, while being cheaper to run because it was smaller. Their fitted loss had the form

    L(N, D) = E + A / N^alpha + B / D^beta

where E is an irreducible loss (the entropy of natural text), and the other terms are the extra loss from finite model size and finite data.

After Chinchilla, models were trained on far more data. Meta's LLaMA (Hugo Touvron and colleagues, February 2023) trained models of 7 to 65 billion parameters on about 1 to 1.4 trillion tokens, and later open models went well beyond Chinchilla's ratio (trillions of tokens for models of a few billion parameters), because a smaller model trained longer is cheaper to serve to millions of users, even if training is not compute-optimal. The availability of high-quality text became a concern: estimates suggested that the stock of public human-written text might be largely used by the late 2020s, motivating synthetic data and multimodal data.

7. Emergent abilities and their measurement

As models grew, some benchmarks showed near-random performance at small scales and a sudden jump at large scale. Jason Wei and colleagues ("Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models," 2022) catalogued such "emergent" abilities, including multi-step arithmetic and certain reasoning tasks, and chain-of-thought prompting (Section 19.3) helped only beyond a certain size. Rylan Schaeffer, Brando Miranda and Sanmi Koyejo ("Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?," 2023) argued that many sudden jumps result from the choice of metric: with all-or-nothing metrics like exact match, a smooth improvement in per-token accuracy can look like a sudden leap, and with continuous metrics the same abilities often improve smoothly. Both effects seem real: loss falls smoothly, while particular capabilities can appear abruptly as measured on particular tests. Predicting which new abilities will appear at what scale remains an open question with consequences for safety (Section 20.2).

8. The bitter lesson

In March 2019, Richard Sutton wrote a short essay, "The Bitter Lesson," arguing that the biggest lesson of 70 years of AI research is that general methods that leverage computation, chiefly search and learning, ultimately win over methods that build in human knowledge. Chess (Section 9.3), Go (Section 16.4), speech recognition and vision all followed this pattern. The GPT series and scaling laws were widely read as strong confirmation. Critics point out that scaling has costs (energy, money, concentration of capability in a few companies), that data quality, architecture and training methods also mattered greatly, and that loss on next-token prediction is not the same as reliability or understanding. These debates continue in Chapters 19 and 20.

9. Summary

  - Decoder-only transformers are trained to predict the next token; text is generated by sampling one token at a time.
  - GPT (June 2018, about 117M parameters) showed generative pretraining plus fine-tuning; GPT-2 (February 2019, 1.5B, WebText 40 GB) showed zero-shot task performance and prompted a staged release.
  - GPT-3 (May 2020; 175B parameters, 96 layers, 300B tokens, about 3 x 10^23 training operations) showed in-context few-shot learning.
  - Kaplan and colleagues (January 2020) found loss follows power laws in parameters, data and compute; training compute is approximately 6 N D.
  - Chinchilla (March 2022; 70B parameters, 1.4T tokens) showed parameters and tokens should scale together, about 20 tokens per parameter for compute-optimal training.
  - "Emergent" abilities may partly reflect the choice of metric; scaling's predictability made it the industry's guiding strategy.
